title: The Cost of a Free Event
passage:
Maho's town held a free outdoor music event every autumn. Because no tickets were sold, many residents described the festival as costing nothing. Maho repeated the same phrase until she joined the youth planning team. At the first meeting, the organizer showed a budget containing costs for sound equipment, security, temporary toilets, cleaning, insurance, signs, and electricity. Local companies donated some money, the town provided part of the budget, and volunteers supplied many hours of work. The event was free for visitors, but it was certainly not free to produce. The team faced a difficult decision that year because costs had increased. One suggestion was to reduce the number of performers. Another was to charge a small entrance fee. A third was to ask for more volunteers and donations. Each option had disadvantages. Fewer performers might reduce the festival's appeal. A ticket fee could exclude families who attended because it was free. More volunteers could lower some costs, but trained professionals were still necessary for electrical work, security, and sound control. The team decided to keep admission free but redesign several parts of the event. They placed food stalls closer together so fewer electrical cables were needed, reused signs from the previous year, and shortened the program by one hour rather than removing an entire performer. They also created a donation station that clearly explained what different amounts could support. The station did not pressure visitors; it simply made the hidden costs visible. After the festival, total donations were higher than before. The planning team also recorded volunteer hours for the first time. Maho was surprised to see how much unpaid labor had supported the event. She realized that calling something free often means that someone else is paying with money, time, space, or another resource. This did not make free public events a bad idea. In fact, the team believed free entry was valuable because it allowed many different people to attend. However, understanding the real costs helped them make better choices about what to protect and what to change. The following year, the budget discussion began with two columns: money and other contributions. Volunteer time, donated equipment, and free use of public land were listed beside direct expenses. Maho found that this broader view made debates more honest. People could still disagree about priorities, but they were less likely to treat any choice as costless. She learned that the word free describes what a user pays at a particular moment, not whether resources are required at all.

The planning team later asked whether donations themselves could create a new problem. If a few large sponsors supplied most of the money, those sponsors might expect more influence over the program. The organizers therefore wrote a policy separating financial support from decisions about performers. They also published a short budget summary after the event so residents could see how public funds and donations were used. Maho found that transparency changed conversations. Instead of saying the festival costs too much, people could discuss particular expenses such as security, toilets, or stage equipment. Some costs that looked high at first were connected to legal or safety requirements and could not simply be removed. Other expenses were traditions that could be reconsidered. The team still had to make value judgments, but the debate became more concrete. Maho realized that understanding cost does not force a community to choose the cheapest option. It allows people to know what they are giving up when they choose something more expensive.
translation:
真帆の町では毎秋、入場無料の屋外音楽イベントが開かれていました。真帆も『お金がかからない祭り』と思っていましたが、若者企画チームに入ると、音響設備、警備、仮設トイレ、清掃、保険、案内表示、電気など多くの費用があることを知りました。企業の寄付、町の予算、そしてボランティアの時間によって成り立っていたのです。その年は費用上昇のため、出演者を減らす、小額の入場料を取る、寄付やボランティアを増やすなどの案が出ました。しかし、出演者減は魅力低下、入場料は家族連れの参加を難しくし、ボランティアだけでは専門的な電気・警備・音響作業を代替できません。そこで無料入場は維持しつつ、屋台をまとめて電気ケーブルを減らし、前年の看板を再利用し、出演者を一組削る代わりに全体を一時間短縮しました。また、寄付金が何に使われるかを示すコーナーも設けました。強制ではなく、見えにくい費用を可視化するためです。結果として寄付は増え、初めて記録したボランティア時間も非常に大きいことが分かりました。真帆は『無料』とは資源が不要という意味ではなく、誰かが金銭、時間、場所など別の形で負担している場合が多いと理解しました。それでも無料イベントには、多様な人が参加できる大きな価値があります。大切なのは本当の費用を理解したうえで何を守り、何を変えるか判断することでした。翌年から予算表には『お金』と『その他の貢献』の二つの欄を設け、ボランティア時間、貸与機材、公共用地の無償利用も記録しました。すると優先順位について意見が違っても、どの選択にも何らかの負担があることを共有しやすくなりました。真帆は、『無料』という言葉は利用者がその瞬間に払う金額を表すだけで、資源がまったく不要だという意味ではないと学びました。

企画チームは、少数の大口スポンサーに頼ると出演内容への影響を求められる可能性も検討しました。そこで寄付と出演者決定を分ける方針を明文化し、終了後には公費と寄付の使途を示す簡単な予算報告も公開しました。すると『高すぎる』という漠然とした議論より、警備、トイレ、舞台など個別費用について話しやすくなりました。費用を理解することは最安案を選ぶことではなく、より高い案を選ぶなら何を得て何を諦めるのかを分かるようにすることだと真帆は理解しました。
